During system commissioning, sulfur was loaded as solid pellets into the vessel and melted using the internal heat exchanger piping that circulates hot heat transfer fluid. During melting, a trickle flow of nitrogen was continuously circulated through the vapor space (nitrogen gas enters through the nozzle at one end of the vessel, exits through another and passes through a carbon scrubber before being vented into the atmosphere). During normal operation, when sulfur cycles between in the molten state, sulfur expands by roughly 5-8 percent. During normal cycling, the blanket gas was allowed to aspirate out with fresh nitrogen being pulled in as needed. The small amount of aspirated gases were processed through carbon scrubbers to ensure safe operation. During the initial fill, melt, and thermal cycling of sulfur, the H S sensor at the scrubber exit recorded 0 ppm, 2 demonstrating the effectiveness of the carbon scrubber in removing H S. Figure 43: Photograph of fully insulated and commissioned sulfur TES pilot system Experimental Testing: Figure 44 shows a simple schematic of the sulfur thermal energy storage (TES) pilot prototype experimental setup. The sulfur TES is equipped with several thermocouples on the exterior surface of the tank that are installed at various circumferential and axial positions, and internal thermocouples that allow for monitoring of spatial and transient temperature distribution within molten sulfur during charge, discharge, and dormant modes. The thermal oil heat transfer fluid (HTF) loop is equipped with temperature sensors at different locations namely at the inlet and exit of the TES, inlet and exit of the HTF to process water heat exchanger unit, and at the inlet and exit of the electric heater. The HTF temperature measurements along with the measurement of its mass flow rate will be used to calculate the heat rate in and out of the different components during various operation modes and also to characterize heat loss in the piping circuit. Other sensors include pressure gauge and gas monitoring instruments, all of which are connected to a data acquisition system (DAQ) for data collection and storage. The data from the sensors are recorded at 15 second intervals. Table 8 below shows the design of experiment matrix for pilot prototype testing.
